items.title: L6: Parliamentary questions and ministerial letters
items.source: GOV.UK, Ministerial Code; House of Commons Library guidance on parliamentary questions
items.body: Members of Parliament and peers hold ministers to account by asking parliamentary questions, often shortened to PQs. Oral questions are asked in the chamber at set question times and the minister answers in person. Written questions receive a written answer that is published. Officials in the department draft the answer, but it goes out in the minister's name and the minister is responsible for it. A good draft answers the question that was actually asked, is accurate, does not mislead by leaving out something important, is consistent with earlier answers and public statements, and is written in plain language. Written questions have tight deadlines, so policy teams, statisticians and the minister's private office work to a timetable. If an answer affects another department, for example by touching on its spending or its policy, the draft is cleared with that department before it goes to the minister. Letters from MPs to ministers are normally handled as a priority because ministers are accountable to Parliament and MPs speak for their constituents. If a published answer turns out to be wrong, officials tell the private office straight away so that the minister can correct the record at the earliest opportunity, as the Ministerial Code expects. Ministers do not normally overturn individual decisions on benefits or tax; a reply should explain the decision and the routes of appeal or review instead.

questions.prompt: A draft written answer says there have been no cases. You know three cases are still under review and none has been concluded. What is the best way to word it?

options.text: Say there have been no cases, because none has been concluded, and leave the minister to explain later if asked
State precisely that no cases have been concluded and that three remain under review
Say the information is not held centrally, to avoid giving any figure that could be misread
Give the number of cases in the last year only, because that is the figure most often used

questions.hint: An answer must not mislead by leaving out something important.

questions.prompt: In whose name is a written parliamentary answer published?

options.text: The official who drafted it
The department's permanent secretary
The Speaker's office
The minister's

questions.hint: Officials draft, but the minister answers to Parliament.

questions.prompt: After publication you spot that a figure in a written answer was wrong. What should you do first?

options.text: Tell the private office at once so the minister can correct the record
Wait for the next statistical release to put the figure right
Correct it only if an MP queries the number
Ask the policy team to judge whether the error is big enough to mention

questions.hint: Errors in answers to Parliament are corrected at the earliest opportunity.

questions.prompt: Which weakness would most clearly mean a draft answer needs reworking?

options.text: It uses plain language instead of departmental terms
It cites an earlier public statement the department made
It answers an easier question than the one the MP asked
It is short and confined to the facts requested

questions.hint: The answer must address the question asked.

questions.prompt: Your draft answer says a policy will cost nothing extra, which affects another department's budget. What should happen before it goes to the minister?

options.text: It goes straight to the minister, who can raise it with colleagues if they object
It is held until the other department publishes its own answer
It is shared with the press office so they can prepare lines
It is cleared with the other department, and with the Treasury where spending is concerned

questions.hint: Answers touching another department are cleared with it first.

questions.prompt: Why are letters from MPs normally treated as a priority?

options.text: Because the law gives MPs a shorter deadline for replies than members of the public
Ministers are accountable to Parliament and MPs speak for constituents
Because MPs can direct civil servants to change a decision when they write
Because an MP's letter is treated as a formal complaint against the minister

questions.hint: Priority follows from parliamentary accountability.

questions.prompt: A member of the public writes to the minister disagreeing with their individual benefit decision. What should the draft reply do?

options.text: Explain the decision and how to ask for a review or appeal, without promising it will change
Promise that the minister will personally review the case and write again with the outcome
Say that individual cases are for the agency alone and suggest the writer contacts their MP instead
Tell them the decision will be looked at again if they write in a second time

questions.hint: Ministers do not normally overturn individual decisions; routes of review exist.

questions.prompt: A minister faces oral questions next week. What would officials normally prepare?

options.text: A speech to be read out in full whatever questions the minister is actually asked
A record of how each MP who might ask a question has voted on previous bills
A briefing pack with likely questions, lines to take and supplementary questions
A written answer to be handed round the chamber instead of replying in person

questions.hint: Oral questions are live, so ministers need flexible briefing.

items.title: L6: Writing a submission to a minister
items.source: Civil Service Learning guidance on writing for ministers; Civil Service Code
items.body: A submission is the formal written advice that officials send to a minister when a decision is needed. It usually goes through the private office, which controls the minister's paper flow. A well-built submission has a short purpose statement at the top that says what is being asked and by when, a clear recommendation, a summary of the issue, the options that were considered with their costs, benefits and risks, any legal, financial or handling points, and the next steps. Readers are busy, so the key message goes first and the detail follows, often in annexes. The Civil Service Code requires officials to set out the facts and relevant considerations honestly and objectively. That means presenting realistic options, including ones the minister may not like, and not hiding a risk or an inconvenient piece of evidence. Officials then recommend an option, because ministers expect a clear view. The minister may accept, amend or reject the advice. Once the minister has decided, officials carry out the decision, provided it is lawful, and they keep a record of the advice and the decision. Submissions are cleared by the policy lead and often by finance, legal and communications colleagues before they reach the minister. If a deadline is missed the submission should say what the consequence is, not leave the minister to guess.

questions.prompt: Where should the main message of a submission appear?

options.text: In the closing paragraph, after the reasoning has been built up
At the top, as a short purpose statement and recommendation
In an annex, so the main text stays neutral
In the covering email only

questions.hint: Busy readers need the point first.

questions.prompt: You prefer option B, but the minister is known to dislike it. How should you write the options section?

options.text: Leave option B out of the submission so the minister does not reject the whole paper
Describe all the options, but present the minister's favoured option as the recommendation
Set out all realistic options fairly, including B with its risks, and recommend your preferred option
Include only the minister's preferred option and mention B in a private conversation

questions.hint: The Code requires an honest, objective account of options.

questions.prompt: A submission should include a deadline. Why?

options.text: It shows the minister when a decision is needed and what happens if it is missed
It sets the date by which the minister is required by law to reply to officials
It lets the private office decide which ministers should receive the paper
It prevents anyone from amending the paper after that date has passed

questions.hint: The deadline and its consequence allow the minister to prioritise.

questions.prompt: Who normally manages the flow of papers to a minister?

options.text: The department's press office
The Treasury
The special adviser's team
The minister's private office

questions.hint: Private offices control the minister's paper flow.

questions.prompt: Which practice best fits a good submission?

options.text: A neutral list of facts with no recommendation, to avoid influencing the minister
A recommendation with the risks left to a separate verbal briefing
A clear recommendation backed by options with costs, benefits and risks
A long chronology of events with the decision requested on the last page

questions.hint: Ministers expect officials to recommend.

questions.prompt: A minister rejects your recommended option and chooses another that is lawful and within the department's budget. What should officials do?

options.text: Delay implementation until the minister reconsiders
Record the advice and decision, then implement the minister's choice
Ask the permanent secretary to overrule the decision
Implement it but tell the press the department advised against

questions.hint: Officials advise, ministers decide, officials deliver lawful decisions.

questions.prompt: Why would a submission normally be cleared by finance and legal colleagues?

options.text: Because they have to co-sign every ministerial decision before it takes effect
So that they can change the recommendation if they disagree with the policy team
Because ministers are not allowed to receive advice from policy teams on their own
To check cost, affordability and lawfulness before the minister relies on it

questions.hint: Clearance reduces the risk of unlawful or unaffordable decisions.

questions.prompt: An important risk is uncertain and no one can quantify it. How should the submission treat it?

options.text: State it plainly with what is known and unknown, not leave it out
Leave it out of the paper until someone can measure it with confidence
Mention it in an annex without saying how serious it could be
Describe it as low risk so the minister is not distracted from the main decision

questions.hint: Uncertainty must be shown honestly, not hidden.

items.title: L6: Handling a Freedom of Information request
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000; ICO guidance for public authorities
items.body: The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives anyone the right to ask a public authority for recorded information. The request must be in writing, give a name and an address for reply, which can be an email address, and describe the information wanted. The requester does not have to say why they want it and does not need to mention the Act. The authority must normally reply within 20 working days. It has two duties: to say whether it holds the information and, if it does, to supply it. Requests are treated as applicant-blind, meaning the answer must not depend on who is asking. Some information is exempt, for example personal data of others, information that would prejudice national security or commercial interests, and some information used to formulate government policy. Many exemptions are qualified, which means the authority must weigh the public interest in disclosure against the public interest in withholding. A request can be refused if the cost of finding the information would exceed an appropriate limit, set at 600 pounds for central government, or if it is vexatious. The authority must offer advice and assistance, for example by suggesting how to narrow a broad request. If the requester is unhappy they can ask for an internal review and then complain to the Information Commissioner's Office. Staff who receive a request should pass it quickly to the team that handles them.

questions.prompt: An email arrives asking for a copy of a department's guidance on a topic. It does not mention the Freedom of Information Act. What is the position?

options.text: It is not valid unless it names the Freedom of Information Act in the text
It is valid only if the sender explains why they want the information
It is still a valid request if it is in writing, gives a name and address and describes the information
It is valid only if it is sent by post rather than by email

questions.hint: The requester need not mention the Act or give a reason.

questions.prompt: What is the normal time limit for responding to a request?

options.text: 20 working days
20 calendar days
One month from the date of receipt
10 working days

questions.hint: The Act sets 20 working days.

questions.prompt: A reporter asks for information that you would happily release to a member of the public. Should the answer differ because they are a reporter?

options.text: Journalists get a fuller response, so that the department avoids criticism
Journalists are limited to information already published on GOV.UK
Requests from reporters must be approved by the press office before any answer is given
The response is applicant-blind, so it should not depend on who is asking

questions.hint: FOI responses should not depend on the identity of the requester.

questions.prompt: A request is so broad that finding the information would cost more than the appropriate limit. What should the authority do first?

options.text: Ignore it, because a request this large cannot be answered under the Act
Offer advice and assistance on narrowing the request
Pass it to the requester's MP so they can narrow it
Reply that the request is vexatious and close the case

questions.hint: Authorities must help requesters refine a request.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when an exemption is qualified?

options.text: The exemption can only be used with the minister's written agreement in each case
The authority must weigh the public interest in disclosure against withholding
The exemption applies only to certain departments listed in the Act
The exemption lapses after twelve months and has to be renewed

questions.hint: A public interest test applies to qualified exemptions.

questions.prompt: Which body can a requester complain to after an internal review?

options.text: The Information Commissioner's Office
The Civil Service Commission, which hears complaints about information rights
The National Audit Office, which audits how departments handle requests
The Cabinet Office FOI Unit, which reviews each department's refusals

questions.hint: The ICO regulates the Act.

questions.prompt: You receive a request in the post office mailbox on Monday and do not notice until Thursday. What is the best practice?

options.text: Wait for the weekly FOI meeting so that the team can decide who owns it
Count the days from the date you first opened it rather than the date it arrived
Reply yourself with whatever you can find quickly to save the team time
Log it with the date it was received and pass it to the FOI team immediately

questions.hint: The clock starts on receipt, so route requests quickly.

questions.prompt: A request asks for the advice officials gave a minister on a policy that is still being developed. What should the FOI team consider?

options.text: Whether the minister has agreed to the request being answered at all
Whether the person asking is a journalist or a private individual
Whether the policy-formulation exemption applies and, if qualified, where the public interest lies
Whether the advice is over a year old, after which it must be released

questions.hint: The exemption is qualified, so the public interest test applies.

items.title: L6: Subject access requests and personal data
items.source: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018; ICO right of access guidance
items.body: Under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, people have the right to see the personal data an organisation holds about them. A request for this is called a subject access request, or SAR. It does not have to use the term and can be made verbally or in writing. The organisation must normally reply within one month of receiving it and cannot usually charge a fee. It may ask for proof of identity, but only what is reasonably needed, and the time limit can start once it has that proof. The person is entitled to a copy of their data and certain information, such as why it is processed and who it is shared with. A SAR is different from a Freedom of Information request. A SAR is about the requester's own personal data, whereas FOI is about information in general and is open to anyone. If a document also contains information about other people, for example a colleague's name in a case note, the department must consider whether to remove it or whether it is reasonable to release it without their consent. Some exemptions exist, for example where releasing data would prejudice the prevention of crime. Staff should never give out someone's personal data to a third party, even a relative, without a lawful basis. The Information Commissioner's Office is the regulator, and a person can complain to it if they are unhappy.

questions.prompt: Someone phones to ask for all the personal information your office holds about them. Is this a valid subject access request?

options.text: It cannot be valid, because a subject access request must be made on the official form
It cannot be valid unless the caller names the Data Protection Act in the call
It can be valid, but only after the caller has paid the fee
It can be, because a request does not need to be in writing

questions.hint: SARs can be made verbally.

questions.prompt: What is the normal time limit for answering a SAR?

options.text: 20 working days
Three months
One month
Five working days

questions.hint: The UK GDPR sets one month, extendable in some cases.

questions.prompt: A SAR arrives and you are not sure the requester is who they say. What is the right step?

options.text: Ask for proof of identity, limited to what is reasonably needed
Refuse the request until the person attends in person with three forms of ID
Release the data and trust that the person asking is who they say they are
Ask them to explain why they want the information before you go further

questions.hint: Identity may be checked, proportionately.

questions.prompt: Which request is a subject access request rather than an FOI request?

options.text: A journalist asks how many cases the department closed last year
A claimant asks for a copy of the notes held about their own case
A charity asks for the department's complaints policy
A student asks for a list of all offices in Wales

questions.hint: SARs concern the requester's own personal data.

questions.prompt: A case note you must release also names a colleague and includes their comments. What should you consider?

options.text: Release the whole file as it stands, since the requester is entitled to everything in it
Refuse the entire request until the colleague has given written agreement
Whether to redact or release the colleague's data after weighing their interests
Delete the colleague's comments from the original record before release

questions.hint: Third-party data requires a balancing decision, not automatic release.

questions.prompt: A claimant's sister phones and asks for details of the claimant's payment. What should you do?

options.text: Tell her, since she is family and clearly worried about the payment
Tell her the amount but not the dates, which are less sensitive
Ask her the claimant's date of birth and, if it matches, confirm the details
Not disclose it unless there is a lawful basis such as consent or authority on file

questions.hint: Personal data goes to a third party only on a lawful basis.

questions.prompt: May a department normally charge a fee for dealing with a SAR?

options.text: A fixed fee of a few pounds can always be charged
Not usually; requests are normally free of charge
A fee can be charged if the data is held on paper
A fee can be charged if the request arrives by email

questions.hint: Requests are generally free.

questions.prompt: Where can a person complain if they believe the department handled their SAR wrongly?

options.text: The Information Commissioner's Office
The Civil Service Commission
The department's permanent secretary only
The Treasury

questions.hint: The ICO regulates data protection.

items.title: L6: Declaring interests when recruiting and buying
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Managing Public Money
items.body: A conflict of interest arises when a personal relationship or interest could, or could appear to, influence an official decision. The Civil Service Code's integrity value requires civil servants to declare conflicts and not to use their position for private gain. In recruitment, the Civil Service Commission's Recruitment Principles require selection on merit following fair and open competition. If a friend, relative or former colleague applies for a job on your panel, you declare the connection to the chair or recruiting manager and step away from sifting, interviewing and scoring that candidate, and often from the whole campaign. The same principle applies to buying goods and services. Public procurement must be fair and transparent and must offer value for money. If your spouse works for a bidder, or you own shares in a company that tenders, you declare it and have no part in evaluating bids. Declarations are recorded, usually on a register held by the line manager or a governance team, and managers decide how to manage the risk. A perceived conflict can be as damaging as a real one because it undermines public confidence. A declaration is not an admission of wrongdoing and failing to declare is the problem. Interests need to be updated if circumstances change. If someone else seems to have an undeclared conflict, you should raise it with your line manager or through the routes in the Code.

questions.prompt: A friend applies for a job on a panel you sit on. What should you do?

options.text: Declare the connection and step away from assessing them
Carry on and score them, but mark them extra strictly to avoid any favouritism
Say nothing, because friends do not count as close family for this purpose
Ask your friend to withdraw their application to protect the panel

questions.hint: A declared conflict avoids both real and perceived bias.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a declared conflict is correct?

options.text: It proves that the official has behaved improperly in some way
It removes the official from the department while the matter is checked
It is recorded so that the manager can decide how to manage the risk
It needs to be made only once, when the person joins the Civil Service

questions.hint: Declaring is the right action, not an admission.

questions.prompt: Your partner works for a company bidding for a department contract. You are not on the evaluation team. What should you do?

options.text: Do nothing, because you have no part in evaluating the bids
Ask your partner to withdraw the company's bid to keep things clean
Wait until the contract has been awarded and declare it then
Declare it so the manager can consider whether any safeguards are needed

questions.hint: Even indirect connections should be declared.

questions.prompt: Why can a perceived conflict of interest be as serious as a real one?

options.text: It automatically counts as a criminal offence under the Bribery Act
It undermines public confidence in the fairness of decisions
It means the competition must always be re-run from the start
It is easier to prove than a real conflict, so it is treated more seriously

questions.hint: The appearance of bias damages trust.

questions.prompt: After joining a procurement team, you inherit shares in a supplier that bids for work. What should you do?

options.text: Declare the shareholding and keep out of any evaluation involving that supplier
Sell the shares quickly and say nothing, since the problem is then gone
Keep it private because you did not choose to inherit them
Ask the supplier to withdraw from the bidding to avoid the conflict

questions.hint: Declare changes in circumstances as they arise.

questions.prompt: Which principle must Civil Service recruitment follow under the Commission's Recruitment Principles?

options.text: Selection by the line manager's preference after an informal chat
Selection based on length of service in the department
Selection of people already known to the recruiting team
Selection on merit following fair and open competition

questions.hint: Merit and open competition underpin Civil Service recruitment.

questions.prompt: You suspect a colleague has not declared a relationship with a bidder. What is the best first step?

options.text: Confront them in front of the team so that it is dealt with openly
Raise it with your line manager or another route set out in the Code
Say nothing until you have proof of what they intended
Tell the bidder you have concerns about the colleague's role

questions.hint: The Code provides routes for raising concerns.

questions.prompt: How often should an official review their declared interests?

options.text: Only when moving to a higher grade in the department
Only if a supplier asks for confirmation of them
Whenever circumstances change, as well as at regular checks
Once, when joining, because interests rarely change afterwards

questions.hint: Interests must be kept up to date.

items.title: L6: Leaks, the press and social media
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Social Media Guidance; Official Secrets Act 1989
items.body: The Civil Service Code requires civil servants not to disclose official information without authority and not to misuse information they have gained through work. This duty continues after leaving the Civil Service. Departments have press offices and only authorised spokespeople speak on behalf of the department. If a journalist contacts you directly, you should not comment, you should take their details and pass them to the press office. A leak is an unauthorised disclosure of official information, whether to the media, a lobbyist or on a social media account. Leaks can breach the Code, the Official Secrets Act 1989 in serious cases, and a department's disciplinary rules. They also damage trust between ministers and officials and between the department and the public. Personal use of social media is allowed, but the Code still applies. Civil servants should be careful not to post anything that suggests party political bias, discloses sensitive information, or could bring the Civil Service into disrepute. Using a personal account to criticise ministers or promote a party, especially from a visible grade or role, can breach impartiality. Statements that your views are personal do not remove the Code's duties. If you are unsure whether something is acceptable, ask your line manager or the department's guidance team before posting. If you are asked to use official channels for political purposes, you should raise it.

questions.prompt: A journalist phones your desk and asks about a policy under development. What should you do?

options.text: Give a brief off-the-record view to be helpful
Not comment, take their details and pass them to the press office
Confirm what is likely to be in the policy so the story is accurate
Refer them to a named senior colleague who knows the area

questions.hint: Only authorised spokespeople speak for the department.

questions.prompt: Which action would be a leak?

options.text: Answering a customer's query using published guidance
Briefing a minister on a draft policy
Sending an unreleased policy document to a lobbyist
Sharing meeting notes with colleagues who need them

questions.hint: A leak is unauthorised disclosure of official information.

questions.prompt: On leaving the Civil Service, does the duty not to disclose official information end?

options.text: It continues after you leave
It ends once you have left the department
It ends once a year has passed
It continues only for staff who held senior grades

questions.hint: The confidentiality duty is not limited to employment.

questions.prompt: You post on your personal social media account that the government is incompetent. You say these are only your own views. What is the position?

options.text: It is fine, because a clear statement that the views are personal protects you
It is allowed because you have not named your employer on the account
It is allowed at every grade, since personal accounts are outside the Code
It may still breach the Code, as impartiality and discretion apply despite the disclaimer

questions.hint: The Code applies off duty too, especially to public criticism of ministers.

questions.prompt: What is the first step if you are unsure whether a social media post would be acceptable?

options.text: Ask your line manager or the department's guidance team
Post it and delete it if anyone raises a concern afterwards
Ask a friend working in another department what they think
Post it from an anonymous account so it cannot be traced to you

questions.hint: Check before posting, not afterward.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about reporting a leak you witness?

options.text: You should leave it to the press office
You should report it to your line manager or security team
You should leave it, as only the person who leaked it must act
You should tell the journalist to hold the story

questions.hint: Leaks are reported through the department's channels.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a leak to the press is acceptable because it exposes a poor decision. What best describes the Civil Service Code position?

options.text: It is acceptable if the decision really was poor and the public deserves to know
It is acceptable provided the minister is not named in the story
Concerns should go through the Code's routes, not to the media
It is acceptable once the decision has been taken and cannot be changed

questions.hint: The Code provides internal and Commission routes.

questions.prompt: Which kind of post is most likely to cause an impartiality problem?

options.text: Posting a photo from your holiday on a public account
Sharing a published GOV.UK job advert with your followers
Congratulating a colleague publicly on their promotion
Campaigning for a political party under your own name

questions.hint: Visible party political activity threatens impartiality.

items.title: L6: Raising a concern step by step
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Commission, Raising a concern under the Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
items.body: The Civil Service Code says that if you are asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Code, or you see others doing so, you should report it. The process has stages. First, raise the matter with your line manager or someone else in your management chain. Departments also have a nominated officer, sometimes called a nominated officer or whistleblowing officer, who can hear concerns confidentially, and a staff helpline or integrity route. If you do not think the matter has been dealt with properly, you can ask the department to look again. If it still is not resolved, you can take it to the Civil Service Commission, an independent body set up in law. The Commission can accept a complaint only after the department's own process has been used, unless there is a good reason. It considers whether there has been a breach of the Code and can make recommendations to the department. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 also protects workers who make a protected disclosure about wrongdoing, such as a crime, a failure to meet a legal duty or danger to health and safety, from being dismissed or treated badly. Concerns should be raised in good faith, with the facts you actually have, not guessed. Keep a note of what you saw, when and who you told. Do not investigate it yourself or confront the person, and keep the matter confidential so the process is not undermined.

questions.prompt: You have seen a manager approving payments without the required checks. Who do you normally approach first?

options.text: The Civil Service Commission, since it is independent of the department
Your line manager or someone in your management chain
The National Audit Office, since it examines how money is spent
A journalist, since the public should hear about it quickly

questions.hint: Raise the concern internally first.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a nominated officer?

options.text: To hear concerns confidentially and advise on the process
To decide whether a minister has breached the Ministerial Code
To investigate every concern personally
To approve staff transfers

questions.hint: Nominated officers provide an independent point of contact.

questions.prompt: When can you normally take a concern to the Civil Service Commission?

options.text: At any time, even before telling anyone inside your department
Only once the matter has become public and been reported in the press
Only after you have left the Civil Service and are free to speak
After the department's own process has been followed, unless there is good reason not to

questions.hint: The Commission is usually the last stage.

questions.prompt: What can the Civil Service Commission do if it finds that the Code was breached?

options.text: Dismiss the official responsible for the breach
Fine the department for the breach of the Code
Make recommendations to the department
Overrule the minister's decision on the matter

questions.hint: It recommends and reports, it does not discipline.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you do when raising a concern?

options.text: Carry out your own investigation first so you are sure of the facts
Tell colleagues so they can back up what you say
Keep a note of what you saw, when it happened and who you told
Wait until you can prove why the manager is doing it

questions.hint: Factual notes support a concern.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 provide?

options.text: Protection for workers who make a protected disclosure from being treated badly
A financial reward for staff who report wrongdoing in their workplace
A duty on every employer to publish all complaints it receives
A right to bypass the employer's process and go straight to the press

questions.hint: The Act protects workers in qualifying disclosures.

questions.prompt: A colleague suggests you let it go because a complaint could harm your career. Which response fits the Code best?

options.text: Let it go this time and raise it only if it happens again
Raise the concern through the proper route, knowing there is legal protection
Tell the press instead, since the department may close ranks
Raise it anonymously with the whole team so that everyone knows

questions.hint: The Code expects concerns to be raised and protected.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether a concern is serious enough. What should you do?

options.text: Do nothing in case you turn out to be wrong about it
Wait to see whether it happens again before saying anything
Ask the person involved to confirm whether they did anything wrong
Talk to the nominated officer or helpline for confidential advice

questions.hint: Confidential advice helps you decide.

items.title: L6: Who answers to Parliament
items.source: Cabinet Office, Cabinet Manual; Managing Public Money; Osmotherly Rules
items.body: The UK constitution rests on ministerial responsibility. Ministers are accountable to Parliament for the policies, decisions and actions of their department, including those carried out by officials. They explain and defend them in the chamber, answer questions and appear before select committees. Civil servants are accountable to ministers, not directly to Parliament, and officials who appear before a select committee do so on behalf of their minister. The Osmotherly Rules set out how officials should help committees. However, the permanent secretary is the department's accounting officer, personally responsible to Parliament for the propriety, regularity, value for money and feasibility of how the department's money is spent. The accounting officer can be called before the Public Accounts Committee to explain it. The same logic applies to executive agencies: the chief executive is the accounting officer for the agency, and the minister remains answerable for the agency's policy. Select committees, one for each main department, scrutinise a department's policy, spending and administration. They can call ministers and officials, take written evidence and publish reports to which the government normally responds within a set period, usually two months. The National Audit Office audits public spending for Parliament and reports to the Public Accounts Committee. Officials should be open with committees and not mislead them, and they should refer questions about policy decisions to the minister.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable to Parliament for the decisions of a ministerial department?

options.text: The most senior official only
The Civil Service Commission
The minister in charge
The Prime Minister's principal private secretary

questions.hint: Ministerial responsibility rests with ministers.

questions.prompt: An official gives evidence to a select committee on the department's policy. On whose behalf do they usually speak?

options.text: Their own personal view
The committee chair's
The permanent secretary's alone
The minister's

questions.hint: Officials appear on behalf of their minister.

questions.prompt: What is a departmental accounting officer personally answerable for?

options.text: Propriety, regularity, value for money and feasibility of the department's spending
Choosing the department's policy priorities on behalf of the minister
Approving every ministerial speech made on the department's behalf
Appointing all the board members of the department's arm's length bodies

questions.hint: That is the accounting officer's role.

questions.prompt: Which body scrutinises the value for money of public spending on Parliament's behalf?

options.text: The Treasury, which approves all departmental spending in advance
The National Audit Office, which reports to the Public Accounts Committee
The Information Commissioner's Office, which regulates public bodies
The Civil Service Commission, which checks how departments recruit

questions.hint: The NAO audits and the PAC examines.

questions.prompt: A committee asks an official why the minister chose a policy. How should the official respond?

options.text: Defend the policy as if it were their own decision
Decline to attend, because policy questions are for ministers only
Explain the advice and facts but leave the choice of policy to the minister
Give their own personal opinion of whether the policy is right

questions.hint: Officials explain; ministers justify policy.

questions.prompt: Who is normally accountable for the spending of an executive agency?

options.text: The local MP, since the agency serves their constituents
The Chancellor of the Exchequer, who sets the agency's budget
The head of the Civil Service, who oversees all agencies
The agency's chief executive as its accounting officer

questions.hint: Chief executives account for their agencies.

questions.prompt: What is the role of select committees?

options.text: To scrutinise a department's policy, spending and administration
To approve appointments made within a department
To manage the department's budget during the year
To draft legislation for the department's minister

questions.hint: Select committees examine departments.

questions.prompt: An official knowingly gives a committee a misleading answer. How does the Code treat this?

options.text: It is acceptable if the minister has agreed to the wording
It is a breach of the Code, which prohibits misleading Parliament
It is acceptable if the answer is technically true
It is acceptable if the committee did not ask the question directly

questions.hint: The Code forbids misleading Parliament.

items.title: L6: Sponsor departments and arm's length bodies
items.source: Cabinet Office, Classification of public bodies guidance; Managing Public Money
items.body: Many public services are delivered by bodies that are not part of the core department. A sponsor department is the department that is responsible for overseeing a particular arm's length body, or ALB. The relationship is usually set out in a document: an executive agency has a framework document, while a non-departmental public body has a framework document or a management statement and financial memorandum. These documents set out roles, objectives, funding, reporting and how much freedom the body has. A chief executive normally runs the body day to day and is its accounting officer. A board, with a chair, provides challenge and governance. The sponsor department has a sponsorship team that monitors performance, reviews risks and holds regular meetings, but it should not run the body's day-to-day work. The minister in the sponsor department is accountable to Parliament for the ALB's overall framework and funding, but not usually for every operational decision. Some bodies must be independent in certain matters, for example regulators and tribunals, and the minister must not interfere in individual decisions. Executive agencies are part of their department, and agency staff are usually civil servants, while many non-departmental public bodies employ their own staff, who may not be civil servants. The sponsor department must be alerted promptly if the body has serious difficulties, so that ministers are not surprised.

questions.prompt: Which document usually sets out the relationship between an executive agency and its parent department?

options.text: A Hansard report
A select committee report
A framework document
A subject access policy

questions.hint: Frameworks define roles, funding and reporting.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a sponsor team in the parent department?

options.text: To run the body's day-to-day operations on behalf of the sponsor minister
To monitor performance and risks and maintain a good relationship with the body
To approve every operational decision the body takes before it is made
To replace the body's board when the board is slow to act

questions.hint: Sponsorship is oversight, not management.

questions.prompt: Who is normally accountable for the day-to-day running of an arm's length body?

options.text: The sponsor minister
The permanent secretary of the sponsor department
The local authority
Its chief executive

questions.hint: Chief executives run the body.

questions.prompt: A minister wants to tell an independent regulator how to decide a particular case. What is the position?

options.text: The minister should not interfere in individual decisions the body must take independently
The minister may do so, provided the instruction is put in writing
The minister may do so once the regulator's board has agreed
The minister may do so if the regulator is publicly funded

questions.hint: Independence protects decisions from political influence.

questions.prompt: Which statement about staff in non-departmental public bodies is correct?

options.text: All of them are civil servants, because they spend public money
All of them are employed directly by the Treasury
Many employ their own staff, who may not be civil servants
All of them are local authority employees seconded to the body

questions.hint: NDPB staff may be outside the Civil Service.

questions.prompt: What should a body do if it encounters a serious difficulty, such as a major system failure?

options.text: Keep it quiet until it has been fixed, so that ministers hear of a solution
Tell the press office first so that the story can be managed
Wait for the annual report and include it there
Tell the sponsor department promptly so ministers are not surprised

questions.hint: Early warning is part of good sponsorship.

questions.prompt: Why does a body have a board?

options.text: To provide governance, challenge and strategic direction
To take all the operational decisions
To report directly to Parliament instead of the minister
To appoint the sponsor department's ministers

questions.hint: Boards govern and challenge.

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of the sponsor minister's accountability to Parliament?

options.text: Every operational decision the body takes day to day
The overall framework and funding of the body
The staff rotas drawn up in the body's offices
The choice of IT systems used inside the body

questions.hint: Ministers answer for the framework, not the detail.

items.title: L6: Devolved and reserved matters in practice
items.source: Scotland Act 1998; Government of Wales Act 2006; Northern Ireland Act 1998; GOV.UK devolution guidance
items.body: Devolution transferred powers from the UK Parliament and government to the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd Cymru (Welsh Parliament) and the Northern Ireland Assembly. Each has its own devolved government. Powers that were devolved include many aspects of health, education, local government, housing and transport, although the exact list differs between the nations. Some powers remain reserved to the UK Parliament, for example defence, foreign affairs, immigration and national security. Employees of the Scottish Government and the Welsh Government are civil servants in the Home Civil Service, while Northern Ireland has its own Northern Ireland Civil Service. Because services in the four nations differ, a rule that applies in England may not apply elsewhere. This matters for customer-facing staff. If a caller from Wales asks about NHS prescription charges, you must not assume the English answer applies; health is devolved and Wales has its own policy. In contrast, a question about passports or visas is a reserved matter and is the same across the UK. Government departments in Whitehall often cover England only for devolved subjects, such as the Department for Education for schools in England. Others, such as the Department for Work and Pensions, cover Great Britain or the UK for most matters. Policy teams must check which nation a policy covers before they advise, and many GOV.UK pages state clearly which nations they apply to.

questions.prompt: A caller from Wales asks whether prescriptions are free. How should you respond?

options.text: Give the English rules, which apply across the whole of the UK
Say you cannot help, because devolved matters are not your concern
Check the Welsh position, as health is devolved and may differ from England
Tell them to ask the UK Parliament directly

questions.hint: Devolved services vary between nations.

questions.prompt: Which of these matters is reserved to the UK Parliament?

options.text: Schools in Scotland
Immigration
Local government in Wales
Housing in Northern Ireland

questions.hint: Immigration and defence are reserved.

questions.prompt: Who employs the staff of the Scottish Government?

options.text: They are employees of the Scottish Parliament as a separate employer
They are employed by local councils in Scotland
They belong to the Northern Ireland Civil Service
They are civil servants in the Home Civil Service

questions.hint: Scottish and Welsh Government staff are in the Home Civil Service.

questions.prompt: Which civil service is separate from the Home Civil Service?

options.text: The Northern Ireland Civil Service
The Welsh Government's civil service
The Scottish Government's civil service
The Diplomatic Service

questions.hint: NICS is separate from the Home Civil Service.

questions.prompt: A policy team in a Whitehall department writes guidance on a devolved topic. What should they check first?

options.text: Which nations the policy and guidance apply to
Whether the Scottish Parliament has approved it
Whether the Treasury will fund each nation equally
Whether the minister has visited each nation

questions.hint: Scope must be clear.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the Senedd?

options.text: A committee of UK ministers responsible for Wales
The Welsh Parliament, with powers over devolved matters in Wales
The Welsh branch of the Civil Service Commission
The council that runs Cardiff and its services

questions.hint: Senedd Cymru is the devolved legislature of Wales.

questions.prompt: Why do GOV.UK pages often state which nations they apply to?

options.text: Because the pages are written by different departments in different nations
Because they are only translated into Welsh and English
Because rules can differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
Because only the English rules need to be shown in the text

questions.hint: Clear scope prevents misinformation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is likely to be the same across the UK?

options.text: Prescription charges
School curriculum
Local bus funding
Passport rules

questions.hint: Passports are reserved.

items.title: L6: Delegated authority and what each grade decides
items.source: Managing Public Money; Civil Service Management Code; departmental delegation guidance
items.body: Authority to make decisions and spend money in the Civil Service is delegated downwards. A permanent secretary, as accounting officer, delegates authority to directors, who delegate to managers. Delegation letters set limits on what each grade or post-holder can approve, for example spending up to a set sum, signing off a contract, or deciding a benefit claim. Delegated limits vary by department, so you must check your own. An Administrative Officer will usually process or check work under guidance and has little spending authority. An Executive Officer may manage a small team or caseload, make some decisions within rules and approve routine spending. A Higher Executive Officer often leads a team or project and has more discretion. Senior grades take on wider decisions, policy advice and larger budgets. The principle is that decisions are made at the lowest level that has the right knowledge and accountability. If a decision exceeds your delegated authority, you escalate it to someone who has the authority. Splitting a large purchase into smaller ones to stay under a limit is a breach of the rules and is sometimes called order splitting. Acting beyond delegated authority, even with good intentions, can cause irregular spending that the accounting officer has to explain. Where you are unsure whether you can approve something, ask before you do it. Keeping a record of who authorised a decision helps audit and accountability.

questions.prompt: Your manager is away and a supplier asks you to approve an order above your spending limit. What should you do?

options.text: Approve it, since the need is clear and the supplier is waiting
Split the order in two so that each part stays under your limit
Escalate to someone with enough delegated authority, such as the manager's deputy or the next level up
Ask the supplier to hold the order without telling anyone, until your manager returns

questions.hint: Decisions above your limit must be escalated.

questions.prompt: What does order splitting mean in procurement?

options.text: Placing one order with two suppliers so that they share the work
Dividing a purchase into smaller ones to avoid a limit or competition rule
Dividing a project across two financial years to smooth the spend
Asking two managers to approve a single order to speed up sign-off

questions.hint: It is a way of evading controls and is not allowed.

questions.prompt: Where would you find the limit on what you may approve?

options.text: On GOV.UK, where all departments publish identical limits
In the Civil Service Code, which lists limits by grade
In the job advert you originally applied for
In your delegation letter or the department's delegation guidance

questions.hint: Delegations are set by each department.

questions.prompt: Who delegates financial authority downwards in a department?

options.text: The accounting officer, usually the permanent secretary
The Prime Minister, in the delegation letters to each department
The Civil Service Commission, as part of its audit role
The chief whip, on behalf of the government

questions.hint: Delegation flows from the accounting officer.

questions.prompt: Why can acting beyond delegated authority be a problem even if the decision was sensible?

options.text: It is automatically a criminal offence for the official concerned
It always has to be reversed by the minister
It is only a problem if the sum involved is over a million pounds
It can create irregular spending the accounting officer must account for

questions.hint: Authority matters as well as outcome.

questions.prompt: Which principle best describes how decisions should be made?

options.text: Always by the most senior person available, to reduce the risk of error
At the lowest level with the right knowledge and accountability
By whoever can make the decision fastest
By whoever first received the request, wherever they sit

questions.hint: Delegation puts decisions where expertise and accountability sit.

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of who authorised a decision?

options.text: It makes the decision binding on the Treasury
It lets the decision be reversed at any time
It supports audit and accountability
It is required only for decisions over £10,000

questions.hint: Records show who was accountable.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether a payment is within your authority. What is best?

options.text: Ask your manager or finance team before approving
Approve it and check afterwards
Ask a colleague at the same grade to approve it instead
Delay the payment indefinitely

questions.hint: Check before, not after.

items.title: L6: Keeping records and an audit trail
items.source: Public Records Act 1958; National Archives guidance on information management; Civil Service Code
items.body: Civil servants must keep accurate records of their work, because records show what was decided, by whom and why. The Civil Service Code's honesty value includes not deceiving anyone and keeping accurate information. Good records help colleagues pick up work, support audit and legal challenges, and allow Parliament, the courts and the public to scrutinise decisions. The Public Records Act 1958 requires government records of lasting value to be selected and transferred to The National Archives after a set period, where they can be made available to the public. Records may be paper or electronic: emails, messages, notes and spreadsheets can all be official records. Official business should be conducted using official systems. If a decision is made in a meeting or call, someone should record the decision, who agreed it and any actions. Files should be named clearly, stored in the right place and given the right security marking. Records must not be altered or deleted to hide what happened. Changing a date or removing a document to make a decision look better is a serious breach of the Code and can also be a criminal matter. A record should be factual and professional, since it may be disclosed through the Freedom of Information Act, a subject access request or legal proceedings. Retention schedules say how long records are kept before review or destruction.

questions.prompt: A meeting agrees to change a policy. What should be recorded?

options.text: The decision, who agreed it and any actions
Only the final version of the policy once it is published
A description of the tone and mood of the discussion
Nothing, because any notes made could later be disclosed

questions.hint: Records capture decisions and responsibility.

questions.prompt: Why should records be written assuming they may be disclosed?

options.text: They are all published automatically on GOV.UK
They are read by the minister before they are filed
They can be released through FOI, subject access requests or legal proceedings
They are always read aloud when the department gives evidence

questions.hint: Disclosure is possible, so write factually.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an official record?

options.text: A private text to a friend about weekend plans
A personal diary kept at home with no work content
A supermarket receipt
An email recording a decision on a case

questions.hint: Official business in any format can be a record.

questions.prompt: You discover that an important document was saved on your personal laptop. What should you do?

options.text: Delete it from the laptop and carry on, since it is now with the department
Move it into the official system and tell your manager how it was stored
Keep it on the laptop for safety in case the system fails
Email it to a personal address as a backup

questions.hint: Official work belongs on official systems.

questions.prompt: Your supervisor asks you to alter a date on a record to make a deadline look met. What does the Code require?

options.text: Do it, since the supervisor is responsible
Do it but note the original date elsewhere
Do it and mention it to a colleague
Refuse, and raise the matter through the Code's routes

questions.hint: Falsifying records breaches honesty and integrity.

questions.prompt: What do retention schedules set out?

options.text: How long different types of record are kept before review or destruction
Who is allowed to read each document and for how long
Which records are published on GOV.UK each year
How many copies of a record the department must keep

questions.hint: They govern keeping and disposal.

questions.prompt: What does the Public Records Act 1958 do?

options.text: Gives every citizen a right to see all departmental emails
Requires every record to be destroyed after one year
Requires records of lasting value to be transferred to The National Archives
Makes ministers the legal owners of all departmental papers

questions.hint: It governs public record preservation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is good file practice?

options.text: Personal initials in file names for speed and simplicity
Clear naming, correct storage and the right security marking
Working copies kept in several unmarked folders for safety
All material kept in one large email inbox so nothing is lost

questions.hint: Findable, secure records support accountability.

items.title: L6: Working with special advisers and private offices
items.source: Code of Conduct for Special Advisers; Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010; Civil Service Code
items.body: Special advisers, often called spads, are temporary civil servants appointed by ministers to provide political advice and support. They are exempt from the requirement for civil servants to be appointed on merit through fair and open competition and from the rule that civil servants must be politically impartial. Their appointment ends when their minister leaves office or a general election is called. The Code of Conduct for Special Advisers sets what they may do: they can advise ministers on party-political aspects of issues, represent the minister's views to the media, speak to party colleagues and commission research. They cannot ask civil servants to do anything which is party political, cannot normally manage permanent civil servants, and cannot use public resources for party purposes. Officials who work with special advisers should keep their own advice impartial and separate from political advice. Officials can share information and support with a special adviser as the minister's representative, but they stay accountable to the minister and ultimately the permanent secretary. If a special adviser asks you to do something that seems party political, such as drafting a party attack line, you should decline politely and raise it with your line manager or the private office. Private offices act as the link between the minister and the department. Officials in a private office handle the minister's diary, papers and correspondence and must serve ministers impartially, whichever party is in power.

questions.prompt: A special adviser asks you to draft a speech attacking the opposition party's record. What should you do?

options.text: Draft it, but keep it strictly factual so that it is not partisan
Draft it, then ask the minister to approve it before it is used
Decline, since civil servants cannot do party-political work, and tell your line manager
Draft it in your own time so that it does not use official resources

questions.hint: Civil servants must not carry out party-political tasks.

questions.prompt: How does a special adviser differ from a permanent civil servant?

options.text: They are appointed by the minister and are not required to be politically impartial
They are appointed by open competition on merit
They stay when the government changes
They are accountable to the permanent secretary alone

questions.hint: Spads are temporary, political appointees.

questions.prompt: When does a special adviser's appointment normally end?

options.text: After exactly one year, whatever the minister is doing
At the end of the financial year in which they were appointed
When the permanent secretary decides that the adviser is no longer needed
When their minister leaves office or an election is called

questions.hint: Their post is tied to the minister.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a special adviser allowed to do?

options.text: Instruct officials to prepare party leaflets in office hours
Advise on the party-political aspects of an issue
Give orders to civil servants about their normal duties
Use departmental funds for party campaigns

questions.hint: Spads advise on party-political aspects.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a private office?

options.text: To link the minister and department, handling diary, papers and correspondence
To manage the department's finances and report them to the Treasury
To audit the department's accounts for the minister
To advise the minister on party strategy at election time

questions.hint: Private offices serve the minister impartially.

questions.prompt: A spad asks for factual information on a policy, which the minister is entitled to see. What should the official do?

options.text: Refuse, since special advisers are not part of the Civil Service
Provide it as they would for the minister, keeping impartial advice impartial
Provide only partial information, so that policy work is protected
Ask the opposition for the same information before replying

questions.hint: Officials support the minister's team within the Code.

questions.prompt: Why must officials keep their own advice separate from political advice?

options.text: To make sure that official advice always carries more weight than political advice
To stop the minister ever using political advice at all
To keep impartiality and ensure the minister receives objective advice
To speed up decisions by splitting up the advice into separate papers

questions.hint: Impartial advice is a core Civil Service value.

questions.prompt: A private office official is told the party in government has changed. What is the right approach?

options.text: Ask for a transfer to a department with a different minister
Wait for instructions from the new governing party's leader
Hold back all papers until the new minister signs a confidentiality form
Serve the new minister as impartially and loyally as the last

questions.hint: Impartiality means serving whichever government is in power.

items.title: L6: The public sector equality duty in everyday decisions
items.source: Equality Act 2010, section 149; Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 includes the public sector equality duty (PSED), which applies to public bodies, including government departments. When carrying out their functions, public bodies must have due regard to three aims: eliminating unlawful discrimination, harassment and victimisation, advancing equality of opportunity between people who share a protected characteristic and those who do not, and fostering good relations between them. 'Due regard' means thinking about the aims seriously, with an open mind, before making a decision, not afterwards. The duty applies to policy as well as service delivery. It is why departments often carry out an equality analysis, sometimes called an equality impact assessment, which looks at how a policy might affect different groups, for example disabled people, older people or women. The duty does not guarantee a particular outcome and does not stop a body making decisions that disadvantage some people, but it requires that the effect on equality is considered, recorded and, where possible, reduced. Keeping a record of the analysis matters because courts can examine whether the duty was properly considered. Courts have said that it cannot be a box-ticking exercise done after the decision is made. Examples of reasonable adjustments in delivery, such as providing information in accessible formats, help to meet the duty. Officials who spot an equality risk should raise it with the policy lead or the department's equality team early enough for it to make a difference.

questions.prompt: What does 'due regard' mean in the public sector equality duty?

options.text: Producing an equality document after the decision, to show the file is complete
Doing whatever an equality group asks the department to do
Avoiding any decision that would affect any group differently from others
Considering the three aims seriously and with an open mind before the decision is made

questions.hint: Due regard is a real, timely consideration.

questions.prompt: A policy team finishes a decision, then writes an equality assessment to put in the file. What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, so long as the document exists on file
The assessment should have been written by the minister personally
The duty must be considered before the decision, not as a later record
The assessment should have been published for comment first

questions.hint: Box-ticking after the event does not meet the duty.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the three aims of the duty?

options.text: Fostering good relations between people who share a protected characteristic and those who do not
Guaranteeing equal outcomes for every group affected by a decision
Giving priority to disabled people in every decision the department takes
Preventing any change in policy that could affect a protected group

questions.hint: Good relations is one of the aims.

questions.prompt: Does the duty mean a department can never make a decision which disadvantages a group?

options.text: The duty bans any decision that has an adverse effect on a group, in every circumstance
The effect must be considered, recorded and reduced where possible, but outcomes are not guaranteed
The duty can be set aside if the minister approves the decision in writing
The effects on groups need not be considered if the policy has a lawful aim

questions.hint: The duty is about consideration, not guaranteed outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why does the department keep a record of its equality analysis?

options.text: The courts can examine whether the duty was properly considered
Because ministers read every equality analysis
Because it replaces the need for legal advice
Because the Treasury demands it for all spending

questions.hint: Evidence of due regard matters in challenges.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would help meet the duty in delivering a service?

options.text: Treating every customer exactly the same regardless of need
Providing information in accessible formats
Removing contact options for those who find them difficult
Setting a single method for everyone

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments help meet the duty.

questions.prompt: You notice a planned policy change could disadvantage older customers who cannot use digital services. What should you do?

options.text: Wait until the policy is live to see if complaints arrive
Assume the minister has already considered it
Leave it to the customers to complain
Raise it early with the policy lead or equality team

questions.hint: Equality risks should be raised in time to influence decisions.

questions.prompt: To whom does the duty apply?

options.text: Only private companies that deliver public services
Only local authorities, but not central government
Public bodies, including government departments, when carrying out their functions
Only the Equality and Human Rights Commission itself

questions.hint: It binds public bodies and those carrying out public functions.
